transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-14
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CISO, Sierra Health), Priya Shah (IT Ops Manager), Daniel Kim (Security Engineer)

Summary (auto): Quick audit-log review focused on admin activity capture, export, retention options, and encryption/KMS considerations. Action items agreed for document and demo follow ups.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Hayes: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE on the account, and Maya is here from our security/infra team. Quick round-robin?
[00:08] Liam O'Connor: Liam here, CISO at Sierra Health. We run a hybrid cloud, and auditability is a hard requirement for our regulated data.
[00:13] Priya Shah: Priya, I run ops. We'll primarily be focused on export and retention flows.
[00:16] Daniel Kim: Daniel, Security Engineer, I'll handle technical testing.
[00:19] Maya Patel: Great, thanks. Today we'll cover what Redwood captures in audit logs, how admin activity is represented, export options for SIEM/S3/syslog, retention and legal hold, and encryption/KMS integration.
[00:30] Jordan Hayes: Just to set expectations — this is a security review call, not a live POC. We'll walk through artifacts and then coordinate hands-on work.
[00:37] Liam O'Connor: Perfect. High level question: do your audit logs capture both API-level events and console/admin UI events?
[00:44] Maya Patel: Yes. We capture request-level events (API calls: model invocations, token usage metadata), admin events (user creation, role changes, policy updates), auth events (SSO logins, failed attempts), and system-level events like cluster scaling and config changes. There are some field-name differences across exports; we'll share the schema.
[00:58] Daniel Kim: When you say admin events, do you capture the before/after state for role changes? We need to prove who changed what and previous role.
[01:05] Maya Patel: Good question. For admin role changes we include actor, timestamp, action type, target resource, and delta payload where applicable — so we store previous and new values for RBAC updates. It's in the admin_activity object in the export. Note — sometimes the auto-transcription here will call it admin activity as two words, and the field might show up as admin_activity or adminEvent, depends on export format.
[01:22] Priya Shah: Is that data stored in the hosted logs for the retention window? We need to know if historic snapshots are available for audit beyond user-facing UI.
[01:30] Maya Patel: For Hosted API, logs are retained for the customer's configured retention window. We have default 90 days for standard plans, and extended retention options (1, 3, and 7 years) as an add-on or part of Dedicated/Private agreements. Exports can be pushed to customer-managed S3 for long-term archival.
[01:46] Jordan Hayes: To confirm, we support both pushing compressed JSON/NDJSON to S3 and streaming to syslog/your SIEM via a connector.
[01:53] Daniel Kim: How do you guarantee ordering and completeness when streaming to SIEM? We can't have gaps in admin events — chain of custody matters.
[02:00] Maya Patel: We provide sequence IDs and checksums in the stream. For streaming connectors we push events with a monotonically increasing sequence per tenant and a windowed ack mechanism. When delivering to S3 we also provide manifest files with checksums so you can validate completeness.
[02:15] Liam O'Connor: Encryption — how are logs encrypted at rest and in transit? We need KMS integration and ideally customer-managed keys.
[02:22] Maya Patel: All logs are encrypted in transit via TLS. At rest, hosted logs are encrypted with our KMS, but we also offer CMEK (customer-managed encryption keys) for Dedicated and Private customers. For S3 exports, we can write directly to your S3 bucket using your KMS key ARN (AWS KMS). For on-prem or air-gapped, we can provide an appliance package or a secure export.
[02:37] Priya Shah: Any HSM integration for key rotation/secure key storage? We use an enterprise HSM for certain keys.
[02:42] Maya Patel: We integrate with AWS CloudHSM and support external HSMs via standard KMIP or custom integrations under enterprise agreement. Rotation schedules can be automated or customer-controlled depending on deployment.
[02:53] Daniel Kim: How do audit logs relate to RBAC and SSO events? If a user deprovisions in Okta, will the audit reflect the SSO event and the effect on sessions?
[03:01] Maya Patel: Yes. SSO events (SAML/SCIM user provisioning, login attempts, SSO failures) are emitted. We also emit session termination events when SCIM deprovisions a user or when an admin revokes sessions. The link is via the user's unique ID and session ID fields.
[03:14] Jordan Hayes: There was a question earlier about map to SIEM fields — we have mapping docs for Splunk and Datadog that map our fields to common SIEM schemas; we'll share those.
[03:22] Liam O'Connor: Retention policy enforcement — if we need legal hold on a subset of logs related to a patient incident, is that supported?
[03:29] Maya Patel: We support legal-hold tagging at the event level. You can apply retention overrides via API or via the Console: tag an event set for preservation, which prevents deletion until the hold is released. For hosted customers, we keep preserved copies in a protected storage pool. For Dedicated/Private, you can enforce retention in your storage backend.
[03:47] Priya Shah: What about PII redaction — do you store any sensitive content from prompts or payloads in the audit logs? We have strict rules about PHI/PII storage.
[03:56] Maya Patel: By default, request metadata is logged (request IDs, model, token counts, latency), but not the full request prompt text unless you enable request-logging for debugging. For customers handling PHI, we recommend disabling prompt retention and only logging metadata. For Dedicated/Private, you can configure filters to redact or hash PII before export. We'll provide the redaction config examples.
[04:18] Daniel Kim: On the schema, can you show an example event?
[04:21] Maya Patel: Sure — high level: {timestamp, tenant_id, user_id, actor_type, action, resource_type, resource_id, admin_activity: {actor, before, after}, session_id, seq_id, checksum} — that's the reference; actual field names vary slightly by export (NDJSON vs. syslog). We'll send the full schema in the follow-up.
[04:40] Jordan Hayes: I'll add that to action items. Also, customers sometimes ask if logs are sent to third-party monitoring. We do have an option to forward to Splunk/Datadog/Sumo via connectors — you'll control the destination.
[04:51] Liam O'Connor: For compliance, we need SOC 2 Type 2 artifacts. Do you have them readily available?
[04:56] Maya Patel: Yes, we maintain SOC 2 and ISO 27001 artifacts; we'll share a redacted report and a controls matrix. For customers in healthcare we have BAAs available under MSA negotiation.
[05:06] Priya Shah: On the export cadence — how quickly are logs available? Near real time?
[05:10] Maya Patel: For streaming connectors, events are near-real time (sub-second to few seconds). For S3 exports we can do near-real-time streaming or batched hourly/daily depending on your ingestion. The manifest approach is recommended for high-integrity archival.
[05:23] Daniel Kim: If we do a POC, can we set up a small sandbox export to our dev S3 with CMEK to validate key usage and integrity?
[05:30] Jordan Hayes: That's exactly what we typically do for security-led POCs. Maya, can we set that up?
[05:33] Maya Patel: Yes — we'll need an S3 bucket ARN and KMS key ARN from Priya. We'll provide Terraform snippets or a one-click console flow to connect. We'll also run a test that writes an export and verifies checksum and manifest.
[05:46] Priya Shah: I'll get the bucket and key — I need the permissions matrix. What IAM permissions do you need?
[05:51] Maya Patel: We need s3:PutObject, s3:PutObjectAcl (if you use ACLs), s3:PutObjectTagging (optional), kms:Encrypt/kms:GenerateDataKey, kms:DescribeKey. We can send a minimal policy example.
[06:06] Liam O'Connor: Audit retention costs — if we keep 7 years of logs for large traffic, what's typical pricing?
[06:11] Jordan Hayes: Cost depends on token volume and event cardinality. For archival we bill per GB per month; Maya will send a ballpark estimate based on your expected daily events.
[06:20] Daniel Kim: Are there rate limits for exporting logs? If we have a burst of events, will some exports be throttled?
[06:25] Maya Patel: For streaming, we can autoscale connectors. For S3, we recommend using batching to avoid S3 request throttles; manifests help verify full delivery. We'll include recommended practices.
[06:36] Priya Shah: How are deleted user events handled — do you retain audit trails if a user is deleted from the system?
[06:42] Maya Patel: User deletion is an administrative action with its own event. We retain historical audit records irrespective of user deletion per retention policy; the events reference the deleted user ID with a flag. For PII-sensitive deletions we can hash or tokenise the identifier in the logs while preserving the event context.
[06:58] Liam O'Connor: For legal/regulatory requests we might need to produce a timeline. Can you produce filtered exports by timeframe and event type?
[07:05] Maya Patel: Yes — we support query APIs and export endpoints that filter by time range, event type, user, and resource. We can generate a forensic bundle with manifests, signatures, and the chain-of-custody metadata.
[07:18] Jordan Hayes: Quick note — some field names in our older exports had slight mismatches; if you plan to consume programmatically, please use the field mapping doc we'll send.
[07:26] Daniel Kim: For the manifest and checksum, what algorithm do you use?
[07:29] Maya Patel: We use SHA-256 checksums and include per-file and per-batch checksums in the manifest, plus an overall batch signature.
[07:36] Priya Shah: If we require HIPAA BAA, is that a gating item?
[07:40] Jordan Hayes: We do sign BAAs for healthcare customers; it's a contractual addendum. We'll route that to legal once the POC progresses.
[07:47] Liam O'Connor: One last thing — can we turn on a read-only admin role for auditors that has limited access to the console and only reads logs?
[07:54] Maya Patel: Yes, RBAC supports granular roles. We have a managed "auditor" role template that only exposes read access to logs and audit exports. You can also restrict IP ranges and enable session recording for auditor sessions.
[08:07] Daniel Kim: Great. Technical ask — can we see a sample NDJSON file with admin_activity entries and a sample manifest?
[08:12] Maya Patel: We'll attach a sample NDJSON and manifest in the follow-up.
[08:16] Jordan Hayes: Alright let's recap next steps: Jordan to send schema and pricing ballpark; Maya to send SOC2/ISO artifacts and mapping docs and sample NDJSON; Priya to confirm S3 bucket and KMS ARN; Daniel to provide SIEM mappings. We'll schedule the export test for week of 2026-07-20.
[08:36] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good, thanks.
[08:38] Jordan Hayes: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up.

End of transcript.
